sources.entry: Build a browser engine in Rust

summary.title: Let's build a browser engine! (Part 1: Getting started)
summary.one_liner: Learn why and how to build a toy HTML/CSS layout engine, starting with DOM tree data structures in Rust.
takeaways: A browser engine (layout/rendering engine) parses HTML and CSS and turns them into on-screen output; the browser chrome is the UI around it.
A toy rendering engine implementing a small subset of HTML and CSS is a practical way to learn the basic rendering steps.
The series starts by modelling the DOM as a tree of nodes, where a node is either an Element (tag name and attributes) or a Text node, modelled as a Rust enum.
Write your own code for the parts you want to understand, and use libraries for the rest; the author's robinson project uses only the Rust standard library.
summary.summary: Matt Brubeck introduces a multi-part series on building a toy HTML rendering engine, which he calls robinson and writes in Rust. He defines browser engine terminology, explains why a simplified engine helps learning, and gives advice on language choice, using libraries, and skipping parts. This first article covers DOM data structures: a tree of Element and Text nodes, with exercises such as extending node types and pretty-printing the tree. It ends with a list of small open source rendering engines for reference.
